newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks heading for more turbulence this week.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks heading for more turbulence this week.

text.p: The Tokyo stock market is likely to be volatile this week, driven by futures-linked trade and racked by persistent uncertainty over the economy and the health of the financial sector, brokers said.

In a bid to assure the market that the government was aware of the turmoil, a top finance ministry official said on Sunday that the economy was in better shape than people thought and urged Japanese to stop selling out their own market.

International finance bureau director Eisuke Sakakibara, dubbed "Mr Yen" for his influence over markets, said in a television interview that volatility in Japanese stocks and yen was due to confusion ahead of fiscal year book-closings.

The benchmark Nikkei average rebounded sharply on January 22, excited by hopes that the government will move to scrap the securities transaction tax, but was unable to keep above the 18,000 threshold for long.

Sakakibara gave his own backing to the moves to drop the securities transaction tax, saying that MOF's tax bureau should consider the fate of the current withholding tax and securities transaction tax in time for the next fiscal year review period.
A securities transaction tax is currently imposed on all deals in stocks, bonds and money markets and analysts say it pushes up the overall cost of financial transactions and hurts market liquidity.

Sakakibara also said although the economy was in better shape than people thought, the financial sector must be ready for a major "bloodletting" as a result of Japan's "Big Bang" deregulation package, and banks in particular will suffer.
But traders said much of the impact from deregulation had already discounted.
"The stock market has already started factoring in the negative effects the 'Big Bang' reforms will have on banks and securities sectors," said a trader at a major brokerage.
"The market is aware that the current number of banks and securities houses will be cut to half as a result of such bloodletting," he said.
Traders said that the banking sector and also construction shares will continue to be sold, as anxieties over bad loans encourage foreign investors to keep positions short.
"In such an environment, investors are only confident to buy blue-chips and shares of smaller firms with strong earnings forecasts," said Haruo Nakaharu, strategist at Toyo Securities.
Brokers said that with the lack of direction coming from the domestic front investors were turning their eyes toward the performance of the Dow industrials and the weakening yen.
"Weakness in the Dow would be psychologically damaging to Tokyo stocks," Yasuo Ueki of Nikko Securities said. "The Dow has been on a bull run which has to stop somewhere."
The sagging of the yen to the 119-120 level against the dollar was also a point of concern, brokers said.
"There is nervousness that foreigners could sell yen-denominated assests to minimise the losses created by a weakening yen," one broker said.
Some said that should the yen fall through 120 to the dollar again, as it did on Friday, strong measures such as an interest rate hike should be considered to stem its fall.
The spectre of higher interest rates would be yet another blow for the battered market.

Sakakibara said in the interview that Japan, Germany and the United States were in agreement on where foreign exchange levels should be, dismissing as "groundless" market talk that differences existed among the major nations.

"There is too much uncertainty hanging over the market," one analyst said. "Investors are hesitant to buy cash stocks, which makes the Nikkei average vulnerable to swings in futures-linked activity, most of which are done by dealers."
